Gremlin
GREM-lin
noun (Silent Generation slang)
Royal Air Force slang of uncertain origin, recorded around 1940–41: a gremlin was an imaginary imp blamed for unexplained mechanical failures in aircraft. American airmen picked it up, and Roald Dahl, himself a former RAF pilot, popularized it in his 1943 children’s book The Gremlins. Since the war any mysterious glitch has been a gremlin.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

When an engine quit for no reason, a gauge went haywire, or a bolt worked loose that every mechanic swore was tight, the RAF crews of 1941 blamed the gremlins — tiny imps who rode along on bombers and made mischief. American airmen picked them up too. It was a joke, mostly, and a useful one: it let tired, frightened men laugh at things they could not control. But the joke points at two deep habits of the human heart. The first is blaming someone else. It is as old as Eden: "The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat" (Gen 3:12). Adam blamed Eve and, in the same breath, blamed God. Scripture will not let us do that: "every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed" (Jas 1:14), and "The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the LORD" (Pro 19:3). The second habit is imagining that the world is run by luck and mischief. The Bible says no little imp runs anything. "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD" (Pro 16:33). Not even a sparrow falls "without your Father" (Mat 10:29). So a Christian can fix the engine, own his mistakes, and rest in the Father’s care. There are no gremlins — but there is a Savior who took on Himself the blame we try to pass to others.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (RAF and American airmen, early 1940s) for the imaginary imp blamed for mechanical failures — a joke that exposes the old habits of shifting blame (Gen 3:12) and crediting luck instead of the Father’s providence (Pro 16:33).

GREMLIN, n. (Silent Generation slang, early 1940s; RAF, then American airmen) An imaginary imp blamed for mechanical failures; any unexplained glitch. "Gremlins got into the radio again."

Decode for families: gremlins are make-believe troublemakers — the real lessons are to own our mistakes and trust God’s care.

Key Scripture

Gen 3:12 — "And the man said, The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat."

Jas 1:14 — "But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed."

Pro 19:3 — "The foolishness of man perverteth his way: and his heart fretteth against the LORD."

Pro 16:33 — "The lot is cast into the lap; but the whole disposing thereof is of the LORD."

Mat 10:29 — "Are not two sparrows sold for a farthing? and one of them shall not fall on the ground without your Father."

Modern Corruption

A joke more than a belief; what it carries is blame-shifting and a playful superstition that hands the world to luck rather than to God’s providence.

expand to see more

The airmen who talked about gremlins did not, for the most part, believe in them. It was gallows humor in a dangerous trade, and nobody should be scolded for it. Still, jokes teach, and this one teaches two bad habits if it is taken seriously.

The first is passing blame, which began in Eden (Gen 3:12) and which Scripture refuses (Jas 1:14). The second is the half-serious notion that unseen mischief runs things. The Bible gives the world a Father instead: the lot falls as He disposes (Pro 16:33), and no sparrow falls without Him (Mat 10:29).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

RAF slang of uncertain origin (c. 1940–41) → American airmen’s word → 1943 The Gremlins (Roald Dahl) → any mysterious glitch.
